strengths: Well-motivated clinical problem addressing annotation scarcity through practical reference-based approach

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple modalities (CT, X-ray, ultrasound) with strong emphasis on out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., 95.41% accuracy on CAMUS ultrasound despite training only on CT/X-ray)
Principled integration of complementary models: VLMs for spatial reasoning and SAM2 for fine-grained localization with clear technical approach
Effective ablation study (Table 4) demonstrating that RL initialization yields superior OOD generalization compared to SFT, suggesting learning of generalizable relational reasoning
Thorough reproducibility support including detailed hyperparameters (Table 5), dataset specifications (Appendix A.2), and clear architectural descriptions
Progressive task formulation (VQA → bbox → segmentation) provides useful insights into component capabilities and model progression
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (VLMs, SAM2, GRPO) with straightforward integration via MLP projection and attention—more a systems contribution than methodological innovation

Incomplete baseline comparisons: primarily compares against SAM2 variants rather than state-of-the-art medical segmentation or other reference-based/few-shot approaches; no quantitative comparison with fully supervised nnU-Net on shared splits
Significant segmentation performance gap vs. fully supervised methods (Dice 0.67–0.75) with no quantitative analysis of annotation cost savings to justify this tradeoff clinically

Unclear data construction contribution: complex DINOv2 matching pipeline (Sec. A.2) lacks ablation; unclear whether performance gains come from method or data engineering; 450k training instances from 413 scans appears artificially inflated

Spatial reasoning claims insufficiently validated: reliance on qualitative CoT examples (Fig. A1) without rigorous analysis of whether model captures genuine relational understanding vs. instruction-following or pattern memorization

Non-uniform generalization: Arcade ID performance drops dramatically for bbox method (41.09% vs. 78.16% for VQA), contradicting strong generalization narrative and suggesting failure on certain anatomical types
Reference image robustness not addressed: no sensitivity analysis for reference quality, anatomical anomalies, or degree of variation between reference and target—critical for clinical deployment

Limited training data diversity: only 2 datasets (RAOS with 413 scans, Arcade with 1,500 images), both similar modalities (CT, X-ray angiography); no training on MRI or other modalities despite OOD evaluation
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or evidence of multiple runs; critical for medical applications requiring uncertainty quantification

Incomplete technical details: optimal transport solver specifications (Eq. 4), curriculum learning schedule for bbox IoU thresholds, and SAM2 memory encoding from reference masks not clearly explained
Minimal failure analysis: OOD results on LERA (61.87% labeling) suggest significant failure mode unexplored; no discussion of hard cases or method limitations
Missing clinical validation: no user studies with radiologists, no quantitative annotation cost-benefit analysis, minimal discussion of deployment feasibility beyond theoretical appeal

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing labeled data scarcity in medical imaging through reference-based methods
Comprehensive multi-modal evaluation across diverse datasets (RAOS, Arcade, LERA, CAMUS) and anatomical targets
Strong out-of-distribution generalization results (95.41% on CAMUS, 61.87% on LERA) suggesting good domain transfer
Systematic three-stage progression from VQA to bounding box to segmentation with clear methodological justification
Empirical validation that RL-based training improves both in-distribution and OOD performance with CoT evidence of reference-guided reasoning
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing models (Qwen2.5VL + SAM2) with standard training procedures (SFT + GRPO); the VLM-SAM2 integration (Eq. 6-7) is straightforward attention over memory, lacking algorithmic innovation

Problematic experimental baselines: comparisons against vanilla SAM2 and per-dataset fine-tuned SAM2-SFT violate the paper's own premise; no comparison with MedSAM, TotalSegmentator, atlas-based, or other reference-based methods despite discussing them

Misleading 'low-supervision' claims: requires 450k training instances from 413 CT scans (unclear data construction), and test-time reference selection mechanism is underspecified; no clear documentation of reference annotation burden at deployment

Unquantified performance gaps: paper acknowledges segmentation quality does not match nnU-Net but provides no quantitative comparison; Dice ~0.7 may be insufficient for clinical tasks like vessel-guided intervention

Limited OOD generalization analysis: only 2 OOD datasets with anatomy/modality shifts (not protocol shifts); no controlled ablation isolating VLM contribution from SAM2 robustness; no failure case analysis
Missing ablations and justifications: no study removing VLM entirely; no comparison of RL methods; architectural choices (LoRA rank, MLP design) lack ablation; why Qwen over other VLMs unexplained

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability stated; no error bars, significance tests, or multiple runs; GRPO convergence and hyperparameter details incomplete; dataset construction from 413→450k instances requires clarification

Weak technical differentiation from related work: insufficient explanation of advantages over LISA, SEEM, EVF-SAM; optimal transport matching (Eq. 4) is standard; 'first to explore' claim sets low bar without demonstrating why this combination is principled

Presentation and clarity: Figure 2 is dense and hard to parse; method split across three sections (3.1-3.3) hampers understanding of unified pipeline; CoT analysis (Appendix A) is anecdotal not systematic

Missing critical analyses: no computational cost comparisons; no sensitivity to reference image quality; no performance vs. annotation budget curves; no discussion of when reference-based methods should be preferred over standard approaches

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine bottleneck of limited annotated medical data; reference-based approach is clinically intuitive
Strong experimental validation with substantial improvements (VQA: 70.68% vs 16.62% baseline; Segmentation Dice: 0.71 vs 0.24), supported by comprehensive tables and qualitative visualizations
Excellent out-of-distribution generalization across modalities and anatomies (95.41% CAMUS, 61.87% LERA), critical for clinical deployment
Logical three-stage technical progression (VQA → Bbox → Segmentation) effectively demonstrates scaling from classification to fine-grained localization
Principled reinforcement learning framework with clear reward design; ablation (Table 4) demonstrates RL improves generalization over SFT, supported by qualitative CoT analysis
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 3 shows superior boundary precision and topology preservation) and reproducibility aids (hyperparameters, dataset details)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—core components (VQA with VLMs, GRPO, SAM2 integration) are established techniques; main contribution is application/combination rather than methodological innovation, with particularly simple MLP adapter design

Inadequate baseline comparisons: SAM2-Memory baseline is weak; missing comparisons with nnU-Net (acknowledged superior but no quantitative comparison), few-shot learning methods, and other prompt-based segmentation approaches; only two medical VLMs compared

Segmentation quality gap acknowledged but not addressed: authors note performance lags nnU-Net (page 8) without quantitative comparison or analysis of clinical acceptability; absolute Dice scores (0.71) unclear for deployment

Methodological design choices lack justification: optimal transport in Section 3.2 introduced without motivation (why better than Hungarian algorithm? no ablation); DINOv2 template matching mentioned but not evaluated; curriculum learning schedule underdocumented

Critical clinical validation missing: no radiologist evaluation, user studies, or anatomically relevant failure mode analysis; segmentation validation limited to pixel-level metrics, missing clinically meaningful metrics (vessel false positives, boundary distance)

Training data ambiguity undermines low-supervision claims: dataset construction uses DINOv2+cross-patient matching+GT filtering, obscuring annotation burden; '450k instances' from 413 scans heavily augmented; unclear whether truly low-supervision

Insufficient generalization analysis: OOD datasets are diverse anatomically but standard medical imaging formats; no evaluation on extreme domain shifts, pathological variations, or pose changes; single reference image assumption not validated
Significant missing ablations: no ablation on optimal transport, MLP adapter design, reference image quality sensitivity, or training set size effects; no analysis of whether multiple references help

Incomplete failure mode investigation despite acknowledged limitation (densely-arranged targets degrade accuracy page 6); no systematic analysis of reference image selection sensitivity or anatomical similarity requirements
Computational costs not addressed: training requires 8×A100 GPUs; inference time, memory requirements for reference bank, and scalability to 3D/video unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated clinical problem: Reference-based spatial reasoning aligns with clinical practice and addresses the scarcity of large-scale annotated medical datasets
Comprehensive experimental validation: Strong OOD generalization across multiple imaging modalities (CT, X-ray, ultrasound, MRI) with substantial improvements (Dice 0.31→0.71)
Thorough ablations and analysis: Multiple ablation studies (Tables 4-5), sensitivity analysis of reference quality (Table S2), CoT inspection (Fig S3), and failure case analysis
Practical benefits demonstrated: 10× annotation speedup with 3-4× click reduction shows real clinical value beyond metrics
Strong baseline comparisons: Evaluation against MedSAM2, LISA, SegZero, and medical VLM baselines with fair SAM2-SFT control
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with effective visualizations and comprehensive supplementary material (28 pages total)
Task-level novelty: First to explicitly explore reference-based identification/localization/segmentation of anatomical structures using VLMs
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components are standard (Qwen VLM + LoRA + GRPO). Optimal transport matching (Eq. 4) and MLP projection (Eqs. 6-7) are textbook techniques. Main contribution is task formulation rather than algorithmic innovation
Overstated 'limited annotation' claim: Trains on 450k RAOS and 21k Arcade samples—reasonably sized datasets. Better framed as 'leveraging unlabeled targets' rather than 'limited annotation'
Small OOD test sets: LERA (87 images) and CAMUS (900 images) are insufficient for robust generalization claims; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals provided
Unjustified design choices: Optimal transport matching necessity not demonstrated—ablation with greedy matching needed. Curriculum learning on IoU threshold (C.3) not ablated
Limited scope: Restricted to 2D images despite medical data being volumetric. No discussion of temporal sequences or multiple references, limiting clinical applicability
Incomplete comparisons: No comparison with classical deformable registration (VoxelMorph) + segmentation pipelines mentioned in related work; no simple template matching baseline
Reference image dependency: Critical dependence on reference quality (92% at LPIPS≤0.4 vs 61% at LPIPS≥0.6); unclear how to select optimal reference images in practice
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability statement; LERA dataset restricted; unclear if results reproducible using only public datasets (RAOS, Arcade, CAMUS)
Unclear SAM2 contribution: Large improvement over SAM2 baselines, but decomposition of credit between VLM guidance and SAM2's inherent capability is limited
Key methodological details in appendix: Reference bank construction via DINOv2 and <Seg> token formulation should be explained more clearly in main text

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple modalities (CT, X-ray, ultrasound) with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation
Strong empirical results on in-distribution benchmarks, with segmentation Dice improving from 0.31 to 0.71 compared to MedSAM2-Memory-Ref-SFT
Well-motivated problem addressing medical image annotation scarcity through clinically-inspired reference-based reasoning
Systematic progression from VQA to bounding boxes to segmentation demonstrates capability and flexibility
Useful ablation studies (Tables 4-5) showing importance of RL initialization and spatial reasoning; shuffled-reference ablation effectively validates spatial dependency
Flexible multi-task interface supporting VQA, bounding boxes, and segmentation for different clinical workflows
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily combines existing components (Qwen VLM with GRPO RL, SAM2 memory integration via standard MLP projection, optimal transport matching from Cuturi 2013) without significant methodological advances

Critically missing comparisons with registration-based and traditional reference-based approaches (atlas-based registration, VoxelMorph, deformable registration) explicitly discussed in related work but not experimentally compared; undermines claims of superiority

Strong performance dependency on reference-target similarity (Table S2: RAOS drops from 92.49% to 61.39% as LPIPS distance increases) is under-discussed in main paper despite being fundamental to applicability

Overstated generalization claims: OOD performance gaps are substantial (LERA 61.87%, CAMUS 95.41% suggests task difficulty varies); 'unseen modalities' framing misleading as training includes CT/X-ray with only ultrasound being novel

Practical applicability concerns unaddressed: no guidance on reference selection, unclear how to handle scenarios without similar references, scalability to large reference banks, or detection of failure modes
Inconsistent experimental setup—VQA trained on RAOS only while bbox/segmentation trained on both RAOS+Arcade—making cross-task comparisons and ablations less informative; justification unclear
Weak annotation efficiency claim (C.6) based on single annotator with only 30 images, no statistical testing, and suspicious baseline numbers (MedSAM2 supposedly requiring 8+ minutes per image)
Missing ablation studies on MLP projection design, comparison of optimal transport versus simpler matching schemes, and systematic analysis of learned spatial relationships
Insufficient engagement with medical imaging domain specifics: limited discussion of projection artifacts, scanning protocols, multi-view constraints, regulatory requirements for clinical deployment
Confusing presentation mixing 'labeling accuracy' with segmentation metrics (Dice/gIoU); massive Dice improvement partly reflects task design rather than purely spatial reasoning gains
No societal impact discussion regarding potential biases, failure modes in deployment, or considerations for when reference-based approach is clinically appropriate

strengths: Well-motivated reference-based paradigm aligned with clinical practice of comparing target scans to reference images
Comprehensive systematic evaluation with three task formulations (VQA, bbox, segmentation) showing progressive complexity and capability transfer
Strong and consistent experimental results with substantial improvements over SAM2/MedSAM2 baselines (Dice 0.67-0.75 on multiple datasets)
Rigorous out-of-distribution evaluation across modalities (CT, X-ray, ultrasound, MRI) demonstrating genuine generalization capability
Thorough ablation studies effectively isolating contributions, particularly shuffled reference experiment confirming spatial reasoning
Practical validation with 10x annotation time reduction and 3-4x fewer clicks required
Extensive reproducibility documentation including hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and experimental details
Clear presentation with effective figures and comprehensive supplementary material
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: paper combines existing techniques (Qwen VLM, SAM2, GRPO) in straightforward manner without introducing novel algorithmic components; contribution is primarily engineering-focused rather than methodological

Fundamental unresolved limitation: strong dependence on reference-target similarity (92.49% accuracy drops to 61.39% when LPIPS increases from 0-0.4 to 0.6-1.0), creating significant practical constraint for clinical deployment without proposed solutions

Inconsistent intermediate task performance: bounding box method shows poor generalization (78.16% on RAOS vs 41.09% on Arcade), suggesting fundamental representation limitations not adequately addressed

Missing direct comparisons with most relevant baselines: atlas-based registration and deformable registration methods (VoxelMorph, registration pipelines) discussed in Section 2.1 but not quantitatively compared despite being strongest alternative approaches

Unclear experimental design decisions: different datasets for different tasks (VQA on RAOS only; bbox/seg on RAOS+Arcade), retrieval-augmented construction never ablated, and inconsistent training scales make contribution isolation difficult

Limited clinical validation: no radiologist comparison, small OOD test sets (87 images LERA, 900 CAMUS), and suspiciously high CAMUS performance (95.41%) suggesting potential task or reference-similarity issues

Underdeveloped reference image selection: no guidance on selecting 'good' references in practice, no robustness analysis for multiple references, assumption of available matched references may not hold in real workflows
Incomplete error analysis: limited interpretation of learned spatial relationships, no systematic analysis of reasoning patterns, failure case insights not provided, ambiguous cases not explored
